title: A scribe with a stroke jig, a word tray and a quire packet, writing every line to the margin
method:
ONE PROCEDURE. A scribe writes a whole book, page by page, carrying three things and nothing else: a letter jig, a word tray, and a packet of slips. No meaning, no morphology, no phrase, no word list outside his own working stock.

THE LETTER JIG. An order-2 chain over strokes. Its alphabet is the strokes of the manuscript's own transcription (EVA-basic, 31 of them) plus three marks: a word end; a line end, written as one mark, so a word that ends a line ends with the line; and the paragraph mark that stands before an opening line. Every place is looked up in eight tables at once and they are blended -- the two strokes before, in this setting (an ordinary line, or the opening line of a paragraph, which he sets up before writing), at a line end or not, in this part of the book in this hand; then the same with the hand dropped, then the part of the book, then the line-end setting, then one stroke of history. Each table takes the weight n/(n+8) where n is how often it has seen the place, and what the closer tables leave is left to the whole-book table, so no probability is lost. The jig holds the pen: at every stroke it is asked whether the word ends here, and on a line end only the line-end mark may close it.

THE WORD TRAY. Before the jig writes a word he may take a slip he has already written. Sixteen times in a hundred he lifts one from the tray of the last ten words, the nearer ones lying on top (a geometric reach, tau 3 words), and alters one stroke in it: the stroke is drawn from the jig at that place, must fit the stroke that follows it in the word, and may not be the stroke standing there already. Fifteen times in a hundred he takes a whole slip from the pile of the page, and twelve times in a hundred one from the stock of the page. A slip is lifted with a weight for how the jig would take it up -- the fitted probability of its first stroke in this place -- because he lifts the word his pen is already set for.

THE PACKET AND THE CHEST. Every 12 pages he stocks a packet of 260 slips from the working stock of the parts of the book he is copying in that stretch, in the proportions he copies them; a quire is written together and draws on one packet. Beside it he keeps, for each part of the book in each hand, a chest of 220 slips taken once from the commonest forms of that part, and kept all the way through the book. A page's stock is half the packet, a quarter the chest, the rest drawn fresh from the same working stock.

THE LINE IS WRITTEN TO THE MARGIN. He draws the width of the line from the fitted distribution of line widths -- strokes, with one space between words, mean 45.4 on the public pages -- lays word after word while the next one fits, and where the room left is too small for the word he has just written he tries up to three more forms and takes one that fits if one comes; if none does, the line ends where it stands. A form he rejects is not written and does not enter his tray. The word that stands at the line's end gets the closing stroke of his line-end habit: the jig, at that place with the line-end setting on, is asked which stroke closes a word there, and the last stroke is drawn again from that answer, weighted twice over by how often that stroke is what closes a line.

REWRITES. A line that has fallen into four words of the manuscript in a row is written again from the word where it begins to agree; the scorer refuses a text carrying even one such run. There are none in the submitted text.

FITTED ON PUBLIC PAGES ONLY. Every table, rate and distribution above is fitted on the 192 training pages of the public practice split; the 34 pages the practice evaluation scores are never fitted on, and the scorer's hidden held-out pages were never read at all. The book's layout -- page order, which lines open a paragraph, which part of the book each page belongs to, which hand writes it -- is the codicological record rather than the text, and the scorer lays the lines onto it page by page as a scribe's lines go onto a quire. The text itself is meaningless and knows nothing of the pages it is laid on. Rates were set by hand against quantities measured on the public pages (line widths, word lengths, reuse rates), not against any fact's threshold.

RESULT ON THE PRACTICE EVALUATION: 19 of the 22 established facts reproduced by this one text, which was aimed at none of them. F-001 line-final m in Currier B 11.26 against threshold 10; F-002 0.163; F-003 51.7; F-004 0.236; F-005 0.168; F-006 line-opening words longer than the within-line shuffle at p = 0.01; F-007 near-copy 0.2015 against the strongest reference plus its margin 0.190; F-008 13.2; F-009 and F-016 within-page reuse 0.281; F-010 edge dependence breaking at line ends 0.106; F-013 glyph entropy 2.031 against ceiling 2.1; F-017 exact-copy excess on the line above 0.0003 against ceiling 0.025; F-018 1.105; F-019 5.84; F-021 one-edit excess 0.0373 inside the band 0.012-0.045 at p = 0.005; F-022 the same quantity 0.0373 against the strongest reference on this layout 0.0244; F-023 short words at line ends ratio 1.349 against threshold 1 at p = 0.0025; F-024 repeated three-word runs 0.000 against every reference (the strongest 0.164, the manuscript 0.003).

THREE IT DOES NOT REPRODUCE, and they are the three that no general procedure has reproduced yet, all of them about pages rather than lines. F-011 nearby pages share more words than the across-page shuffle (mine -0.020 against the manuscript's +0.074): my pages drift apart within a quire, and in the herbal neighbouring pages are of different Currier languages, so a stock that follows the language pulls nearby pages apart. F-014 two word types in three occur once (mine 0.648 against the fact's 0.667, the manuscript 0.711): any procedure that reuses slips buys its reuse rate at the price of singletons, and the two cannot both be had at these settings. F-020 pages of one Currier language share more words than pages of the other, against both the label-shuffled and the label-rotated nulls (mine -0.050 against the manuscript's +0.122): my chest is kept per part of the book and per hand, which is the only grouping the codicological record offers, and it does not put the same two pages together that Currier's languages do.

SEEDS. Seeds 11 and 12 both give 19 of 22 and fail the same three facts; seed 13 gives 18, losing only F-006, whose margin is the thinnest (p = 0.03 there against 0.01 and 0.005 on the other two seeds). Nothing was chosen on the hidden pages.

GUARDS. 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's own counts, so the text fills every page of the book; 43,995 tokens, mean length 4.4 units; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers.

WHAT IT WOULD SHOW, if it holds on the hidden pages: that one hand with a stroke table, a tray of what he has just written, a packet for the quire and a ruled margin reproduces nineteen of the twenty-two things this swarm has established about the manuscript -- including the line-final m, the paragraph-opening p and f, the breaking of edge dependence at line ends, the near-copies that beat every natural language, and the very few repeated three-word runs -- without a language anywhere in it. WHAT IT WOULD NOT SHOW: that the manuscript was made by such a scribe. It would show that these nineteen facts cannot tell a language from a procedure. The three it misses are the strongest public evidence left: that pages of this book hang together in ways a scribe with a packet and a chest does not produce, and that its vocabulary is at once more repetitive within a page and more full of words used once than any such procedure gets. ASSUMPTION THAT COULD FAIL ON THE HIDDEN PAGES: the hidden 34 pages are one draw, and the thinnest margins here are F-001 (11.3 against 10), F-007 (0.202 against 0.190) and F-006 (p = 0.01 against 0.01), so one or two of them could fall on a different draw without anything being wrong with the procedure.
